Task 1

Load in the data that we need:

# DDT data
ddt <- readxl::read_xls("~/Desktop/OU_Masters/Summer_2026/MATH-4753G_Summer_2026/K25936_Downloads/K25936_Downloads/Excel/DDT.XLS")

With this data what we are interested in is the population mean length of the SMBUFFALO fish species denoted as \(\mu_L\). Our Null hypothesis with this in mind is:

\[H_0: \mu_L = \mu_0\]

Where \(\mu_0\) is a mean length we hypothesize the population of SMBUFFALO fish to be.

Part a

We are tasked with deriving the \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) confidence interval for this problem where \(\alpha_1\) and \(\alpha_2\) are the lower and upper tails respectively and \(\alpha = \alpha_1+\alpha_2\). The working of this is below:

We start by choosing a pivotal statistic that is:

  1. A function of the data and the parameter of interest.
  2. The distribution of the pivotal statistic is not dependent on the parameter of interest.

The data we are interested in has \(n=36\), but since the population standard deviation is unknown we will use a \(T\) pivotal statistic.

By definition a \(T\) test (pivotal) statistic is:

\[T = \frac{\bar{Y}-\mu_L}{s/\sqrt{n}}\sim t(\nu = n-1)\]

Then to get our confidence interval we define the following probability:

\[P(-t_{\alpha_1, n-1}\le T \le t_{\alpha_2,n-1}) = 1-\alpha\]

And substitute in our formula for \(T\):

\[P(-t_{\alpha_1,n-1}\le \frac{\bar{Y}-\mu_L}{s/\sqrt{n}} \le t_{\alpha_2,n-1}) = 1-\alpha\]

And then solve for \(\mu_L\):

\[P\left(-t_{\alpha_1,n-1}\left(\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\right)\le \bar{Y}-\mu_L \le t_{\alpha_2,n-1}\left(\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\right)\right) = 1-\alpha\]

\[P\left(-\bar{Y}-t_{\alpha_1,n-1}\left(\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\right)\le -\mu_L \le -\bar{Y}+t_{\alpha_2,n-1}\left(\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\right)\right) = 1-\alpha\]

\[P\left(\bar{Y}+t_{\alpha_1,n-1}\left(\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\right)\ge \mu_L \ge \bar{Y}-t_{\alpha_2,n-1}\left(\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\right)\right) = 1-\alpha\]

\[P\left(\bar{Y}-t_{\alpha_2,n-1}\left(\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\right)\le \mu_L \le \bar{Y}+t_{\alpha_1,n-1}\left(\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\right)\right) = 1-\alpha\]

Therefore we have the \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) confidence interval:

\[\left(\bar{Y}-t_{\alpha_2,n-1}\left(\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\right),\bar{Y}+t_{\alpha_1,n-1}\left(\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\right)\right)\]

Part b

Next we are tasked to make a function that does the following:

  1. Creates a CI interval for a determined \(\alpha_1\) and \(\alpha_2\) pair.
  2. Plots a histogram that is color-coded by whether data points are within the CI.
  3. Performs a test against \(H_0: \mu = \mu_ \pm \epsilon\) by testing if the ball about \(\mu_0\) is within the CI.
ciNonSym <- function(data, alpha , alpha2 , mu0, epsilon, bins, species_name, river_name, quant_name) {
    # Get important values for calculations
    n <- length(data)
    y_bar <- mean(data)
    s <- sd(data)
    
    # Get alpha1
    alpha1 <- alpha - alpha2
    
    # Get critical t-values
    t_a2 <- qt(1 - alpha2, df = n - 1)
    t_a1 <- qt(1 - alpha1, df = n - 1)
    
    # Get ci bounds
    lower_bound <- y_bar - t_a2 * (s / sqrt(n))
    upper_bound <- y_bar + t_a1 * (s / sqrt(n))
    
    # Test our H0
    ball_lower <- mu0 - epsilon
    ball_upper <- mu0 + epsilon
    test_result <- (ball_lower >= lower_bound) & (ball_upper <= upper_bound)
    
    # Plot the histogram and fill by within ci bounds
    df <- data.frame(x = data) |> 
      mutate(CI = case_when(x < lower_bound | x > upper_bound ~ "Out", 
                            x >= lower_bound & x <= upper_bound ~ "In"))
    
    p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = x)) +
      geom_histogram(aes(fill = CI), bins = bins) +
      labs(title = bquote(
        .(paste0(species_name, " Species From ", river_name, " River(s) Tested against ")) *  H[0] * ":" ~ mu == .(mu0) %+-% .(epsilon) * .(paste0(" for ", quant_name)))) + 
      theme(plot.title = element_text(size=12))
    
    # Print the plot
    print(p)
    
    # Return results 
    return(list(
      ci = c(lower_bound, upper_bound),
      t = c(-t_a2, t_a1), # Set lower critical value as negative
      test = test_result,
      ball = c(ball_lower, ball_upper)
    ))
}

We will use the following example to test the function:

df <- ddt |> filter(SPECIES == "CCATFISH")

ciNonSym(d = df$LENGTH, 
         alpha = 0.05,
         alpha2 = 0.02, 
         mu0 = 45, 
         epsilon = 4,
         bins = 25,
         species_name = "CCATFISH",
         river_name = "ALL",
         quant_name = "LENGTH")

## $t
## [1] -2.082331  1.903519

Task 3

We are given the following function:

dendiff <- function(a1,mu = 10, std = 5, alpha = 0.05){
  a2 <- alpha - a1 # non ETI
  qa1 <- qnorm(a1, mean = mu, sd = std)
  qa2 <- qnorm(1-a2, mean = mu, sd = std)
  
  dnorm(qa1, mean = mu, sd = std) - dnorm(qa2, mean = mu, sd = std)
}

#optimize(function(x) abs(dendiff(x)), interval = c(0,0.05))

uniroot(dendiff, interval = c(0,0.05))
## $root
## [1] 0.025
## 
## $f.root
## [1] -6.938894e-18
## 
## $iter
## [1] 2
## 
## $init.it
## [1] NA
## 
## $estim.prec
## [1] 6.103516e-05

First we are tasked with finding the values of \(\alpha_1\) and \(\alpha_2\) for \(y \sim \mathrm{Beta}(3,10)\). To do this we need to rewrite the above function so that it will find the correct root (equal to \(\alpha_1\)) for us assuming \(\alpha = 0.05\):

dendiff_beta <- function(a1, a = 3, b = 10, alpha = 0.05){
  a2 <- alpha - a1 # non ETI
  qa1 <- qbeta(a1, shape1 = a, shape2 = b)
  qa2 <- qbeta(1-a2, shape1 = a, shape2 = b)
  
  dbeta(qa1, shape1 = a, shape2 = b) - dbeta(qa2, shape1 = a, shape2 = b)
}

#optimize(function(x) abs(dendiff(x)), interval = c(0,0.05))

results <- uniroot(dendiff_beta, interval = c(0,0.05))
results

## 
## $iter
## [1] 4
## 
## $init.it
## [1] NA
## 
## $estim.prec

curve(dendiff_beta(x), from = 0, to = 0.05, xlab = expression(alpha[1]), ylab = "Difference in Density", main = expression(atop(Find ~ alpha[1] ~ and ~ alpha[2], scriptstyle(plain("Jason M. Klemm")))))
abline(h = 0, col = "red")
abline(v = results$root, col ="red")

We can then get \(\alpha_2\) by doing:

0.05 - results$root
## [1] 0.04199705

We are then tasked with using a generalized function for Highest Density Interval (HDI) calculations given as the following function:

hdicalc <- function(stem = "norm", args = list(mean = 10,sd = 5), alpha = 0.05){
  
  # function to find the difference in densities
  # Note that this function will toggle to calculating HDI ci's, nr = TRUE (used for newton raphson)
  dendiff <- function(x, nr = TRUE){
    a2 <- alpha - x
    f <- glue::glue("d", {stem})
    q <- glue::glue("q", {stem})
    
    qa1 <- do.call(q, c(list(p = x), args))
    qa2 <- do.call(q, c(list(p = 1-a2), args))
    if(nr == TRUE){
      do.call(f, c(list(x = qa1), args)) - do.call(f, c(list(x = qa2), args))
    }else(c(qa1,qa2))
  }
  # find the root of the dendiff function 
  l <- uniroot(dendiff, interval = c(0,alpha))
  #  Not for NR BUT HDI's
  ll <- dendiff(x = l$root, nr = FALSE)
  # Not for  NR but ETI's
  ll2 <- dendiff(x = alpha/2, nr = FALSE)
  
  list(alpha = alpha, alpha1 = l$root,alpha2 = alpha-l$root, 
       HDI = ll, RHDI = ll[2]-ll[1], ETI = ll2, RETI = ll2[2] - ll2[1])
}

As before we can find the values of \(\alpha_1\) and \(\alpha_2\) for \(y \sim \mathrm{Beta}(3,10)\) as follows:

results2 <- hdicalc(stem = "beta", args = list(shape1 = 3, shape2 = 10), alpha = 0.05)

results2

# Plot for visualization

curve(dbeta(x, shape1 = 3, shape2 = 10), xlab = expression(x), ylab = "Density", main = expression(atop(plain("Beta PDF with HDI"), scriptstyle(plain("Jason M. Klemm")))), panel.first = grid())

abline(v = results2$HDI[1], col = "red")
abline(v = results2$HDI[2], col ="red")
polygon(c(0, seq(0, results2$HDI[1], length = 10000), results2$HDI[1]), c(0, dbeta(seq(0, results2$HDI[1], length = 10000), shape1 = 3, shape2 = 10), 0), col = "red")

polygon(c(results2$HDI[2], seq(results2$HDI[2], 1.0, length = 10000), 1.0), 
        c(0, 
          dbeta(seq(results2$HDI[2], 1.0, length = 10000), shape1 = 3, shape2 = 10), 
          0), col = "red")
text(expression(alpha[1]), x = 0, y = 0.4)
text(expression(alpha[2]), x = 0.5, y = 0.5)
segments(x0 = results2$HDI[1], x1 = results2$HDI[2], y0 = dbeta(results2$HDI[1], shape1 = 3, shape2 = 10), y1 = dbeta(results2$HDI[2], shape1 = 3, shape2 = 10), lwd = 2, col = "blue")
text("HDI", cex = 2, x = (results2$HDI[2]+results2$HDI[1])/2, y = 0.9)

The function gives us an output of the following:

  • alpha: This is the \(\alpha\) level that we defined as an argument for the function and serves as our total \(\alpha\) to get both \(\alpha_1\) and \(\alpha_2\) from. Here we see that we defined it as \(0.05\).

  • alpha1: This is the \(\alpha_1\) value that we obtain from getting the root of our dendiff function. The root value represents the lower tail probability where the difference in density values on our Probability Density Function curve is equal to \(0\), and thus allows us draw a flat horizontal line from one side of the curve to the other. Here we see that \(\alpha_1 \approx 0.008\) and again this represents the lower tail probability for our HDI for the given parameters.

  • alpha2: This is the \(\alpha_2\) value that we get from subtracting the calculated \(\alpha_1\) value from the defined \(\alpha\) value. Here we get \(\alpha \approx 0.042\) which is the result of \(\alpha - \alpha_1 \to 0.05 - 0.008\). Specifically, the \(\alpha_2\) value represents the upper tail probability of our HDI for the given parameters.

  • HDI: This represents the lower and upper bounds of our HDI. Here the HDI is \((0.03594258, 0.45023580)\) for our specified \(\alpha\) level of \(0.05\), so this is the \(95\%\) HDI for the given parameters.

  • RHDI: This is the range of our HDI and is specifically the length of \(x\) that the HDI spans from the lower bound to the upper bound. Here we have the range as \(0.4142932\) and is calculated as \(0.45023580 - 0.03594258\) from our calculated HDI.

  • ETI: This is the Equal Tail Interval and is different from the HDI in that it assumes \(\alpha_1 = \alpha_2\) by taking \(\alpha\) and dividing it into \(2\). This method also relies on the density curve being symmetric which may not always be the case. Here we have the \(95\%\) ETI as \((0.05486064, 0.48413775)\) and is useful to compare to the calculated \(95\%\) HDI. We can see that they are relatively close but not exact which would indicate that our density curve is not perfectly symmetric.

  • RETI: This is the range of our ETI and is specifically the length of \(x\) that the ETI spans from the lower bound to the upper bound. Here we have the range as \(0.4292771\) and is calculated as \(0.48413775 - 0.05486064\) from our calculated ETI.

Further comparing this function, hdicalc, to the one I modified for \(y \sim \mathrm{Beta}(3,10)\) to make dendiff_beta, both return the same values for \(\alpha_1\) and \(\alpha_2\) with the results of those being:

\[\alpha_1 \approx 0.008\]

\[\alpha_2 \approx 0.042\]
